video_title: When Will Bitcoin Go Up Again?
gist: Lava founder/CEO Shaison Meridia tells Anthony Pompliano that Bitcoin's weak price stems from miners and whales (including government-pressured Chinese holders) selling to fund AI and data centers, but that this selling is largely exhausted, leaving a more retail-dominated, decentralized holder base that is still net buying. He pitches AI-profit rotation and a Democratic 'blue wave' hitting AI as Bitcoin catalysts, and describes stablecoin payroll plus Bitcoin-rewards cards as the driver of international adoption; the episode is partly promotional for Lava.

insights.claim: Over the past year, Bitcoin miners and whales sold Bitcoin to invest in AI and data centers, which Lava CEO Shaison Meridia identifies as the main reason Bitcoin has not gone up.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains BTC underperformance vs AI equities as a capital-rotation flow rather than a fundamental break.
insights.quote: over the last year, I would say a lot of whales and miners in particular have sold their Bitcoin to invest in AI.

insights.claim: Meridia says Chinese whales sold Bitcoin over the last year because the government cracked down on both mining and large holders, forcing sales.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: A one-off forced-selling source that, once exhausted, removes supply overhang.

insights.claim: Meridia argues most of the sellers are gone: the biggest crypto exchange was hacked and Bitcoin barely dropped, which he reads as evidence of little incremental selling pressure and an oversold market.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Muted reaction to negative shocks is a classic seller-exhaustion signal worth watching for a bottom.
insights.quote: the biggest crypto exchange get hacked and Bitcoin barely dropped as a result

insights.claim: Meridia says most Bitcoin holders now hold less than $10 million worth, i.e., retail, and these holders are net buyers stacking monthly from paychecks even as price falls, with no intent to sell.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: A more distributed, sticky holder base could lower volatility and reduce whale-driven drawdowns.

insights.claim: Meridia does not expect a 10x in Bitcoin within the next year, instead expecting a matured asset with steadier returns that ideally beats the S&P 500 year after year.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames BTC as lower-vol compounding asset rather than a moonshot — temper cycle-top expectations.

themes.theme: Catalysts: AI profit rotation, blue wave, halving

insights.claim: Meridia expects profits rotating out of AI to need a new home and sees Bitcoin as a primary destination.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Watch AI-equity drawdowns or profit-taking for potential inflows into BTC.
insights.quote: as some of these profits rotate out of AI they're going to need a new place to to put those profits

insights.claim: Meridia argues a Democratic 'blue wave' is likely to hurt the AI industry more than Bitcoin, which could make Bitcoin a liquidity valve capturing capital leaving AI.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Speculative positive-catalyst view of Democratic gains for BTC relative to AI stocks.

insights.claim: Meridia says the halving still matters because it slows new supply, but market structure (seller exhaustion, overextended equity markets) matters more for the next upside.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Weight flow and positioning over halving-cycle timing models.

insights.claim: Meridia claims Bitcoin has clearly won the digital-gold race within crypto and holds an edge over gold because its scarcity is guaranteed in code; he sees older investors buying gold and younger investors buying Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Generational allocation framing for BTC vs gold demand.
insights.quote: I think older people buy gold and younger people buy Bitcoin.

themes.theme: Security FUD and its drag on demand

insights.claim: Meridia says quantum and miner-centralization FUD has deterred institutions and new buyers, but large miners exiting to AI has opened the market to smaller miners, making mining more decentralized and network security stronger.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Miner pivot to AI data centers may be neutral-to-positive for decentralization; FUD clearance could unlock institutional demand.

insights.claim: After hacks such as the Coldcard incident and AI-enabled attacks, Bitcoin holders are re-evaluating custody providers' security, which has paused some buying and caused some losses or sales; Meridia blames 'vibe-coding' companies and expects confidence to recover over the next year.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Security reputation is becoming a competitive moat for custodians; weak-security platforms face attrition.

themes.theme: Stablecoins as an international on-ramp to Bitcoin

insights.claim: Meridia says international users are driving much of Lava's growth: freelancers increasingly choose to be paid in stablecoins over local currency via payroll platforms, then spend them on a Visa card earning Bitcoin rewards, with Lava users in more than 100 countries.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Stablecoin payroll adoption is a rising funnel for emerging-market Bitcoin demand and for card/payment networks.
insights.quote: A lot of the net new users that we see that are getting into Bitcoin are actually coming through stable coins.

insights.claim: Merchant partners including OpenAI, Anthropic, Apple, Google and Amazon fund up to 5% Bitcoin-back rewards on Lava's card as pay-per-revenue customer acquisition; base rewards are 3% in the US and 1% internationally.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows AI companies using performance-based crypto-reward channels for customer acquisition.

insights.claim: Meridia contrasts Bitcoin-only banking with Coinbase, Kraken and Robinhood, which he says use Bitcoin as an entry point to trading, and reports users migrating to Lava after being pushed to bet on every screen at exchanges.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals a user segment rejecting gamified trading platforms — a potential headwind to engagement-driven exchange revenue.

insights.claim: Meridia expects negative regulation to target prediction markets, crypto casinos and crypto trading platforms that encourage gambling, which he calls manipulative, while doubting the Clarity Act would materially help Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Shaison Meridia (Lava CEO)
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk may concentrate on gambling-adjacent crypto and prediction-market platforms rather than Bitcoin itself.
